reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: A restrictive cardiomyopathy caused by eosinophilic infiltration of the endomyocardium, occurring in the setting of persistent hypereosinophilia
Considered the temperate-climate counterpart of tropical endomyocardial fibrosis, representing an earlier, inflammatory phase of eosinophilic heart disease
Underlying causes of the eosinophilia include clonal myeloproliferative disorders, reactive states, and idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome
Endocardial inflammation and thrombus formation typically affect the ventricular apices and subvalvular regions, leading to mural thrombi and embolism
Progression to endomyocardial fibrosis restricts ventricular filling and can tether valve leaflets, producing atrioventricular regurgitation
Cardiac MRI helps delineate endocardial thrombus and fibrosis, while echocardiography demonstrates apical obliteration and restrictive physiology
Treatment targets both the underlying eosinophilic disorder and the cardiac complications, including anticoagulation for thrombus and heart failure management
Systemic features of hypereosinophilia, such as skin, lung, or neurological involvement, may accompany the cardiac disease
reference.pathophysiology: Sustained hypereosinophilia leads to release of toxic eosinophil granule proteins that damage the endocardium and myocardium. Three overlapping phases are described: an early acute necrotic and inflammatory stage, an intermediate thrombotic stage with mural thrombus lining the damaged endocardium, and a late fibrotic stage in which the endocardium thickens and scars. The resulting rigid endocardial layer and apical obliteration impair ventricular filling, producing restrictive physiology, while thrombus predisposes to systemic embolism and involvement of the subvalvular apparatus causes valvular regurgitation.
additionalDifferentials: Cardiac amyloidosis and other restrictive cardiomyopathies
Intracardiac tumour or thrombus of other cause
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis with cardiac involvement
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film confirming and quantifying eosinophilia
Echocardiography for apical obliteration, thrombus, and restrictive filling
Cardiac MRI to characterise endocardial thrombus and fibrosis
Investigation of the cause of hypereosinophilia, including clonality and reactive causes
redFlags: Systemic or cerebral embolism from mural thrombus
Very high or rapidly rising eosinophil counts with multi-organ involvement
Severe valvular regurgitation from subvalvular fibrosis
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends on early control of the eosinophilia before irreversible fibrosis develops and on the extent of cardiac damage. If diagnosed in the inflammatory phase, suppression of eosinophils may limit progression, whereas established fibrosis with restrictive physiology and valvular involvement carries a worse prognosis and may require surgery.
pitfalls: Failing to investigate and treat the underlying cause of hypereosinophilia
Missing early inflammatory disease before fibrosis becomes fixed
Overlooking mural thrombus and the need for anticoagulation
Confusing the restrictive picture with constrictive pericarditis
Not screening for extracardiac organ damage
